cls: Centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant / analgesic
pharm: Muscle relaxant and analgesic (interneuronal blocking agent)

Limited data; use only if benefit outweighs risk
Caution; possible exposure via breast milk

summary: Phenyramidol is a centrally (and peripherally) acting skeletal muscle relaxant with analgesic activity, used for acute musculoskeletal pain and painful muscle spasm such as low back pain. It blocks polysynaptic (interneuronal) reflexes in the spinal cord without disrupting neuromuscular transmission. It is NOT currently FDA-approved (approved in the US in 1960 as Analexin but later withdrawn; still marketed abroad, e.g., Turkey). Clinically important is that phenyramidol inhibits the metabolism of warfarin/coumarin anticoagulants (bleeding risk) and of phenytoin (toxicity risk).
indications: Mild-to-moderate acute musculoskeletal pain and painful muscle spasm (e.g., low back pain/lumbago, neck and shoulder pain)
Adjunct to rest and physical therapy in musculoskeletal disorders

dosage.d: Typically 400 mg orally 2-3 times daily after meals (range 100-400 mg, 3-4 times daily)

dosage.n: Highest documented daily intake ~3200 mg without GI toxicity

admin: May cause drowsiness - do not drive or operate machinery until response is known
Avoid alcohol and other CNS depressants
Monitor INR closely if taken with warfarin or other coumarin anticoagulants
moa: Phenyramidol is a centrally acting muscle relaxant that produces interneuronal blockade of polysynaptic reflexes in the brain and spinal cord, without affecting monosynaptic reflexes or disrupting neuromuscular transmission, thereby breaking the pain-spasm cycle. The parent molecule (not its metabolites) drives the effect. It also has intrinsic analgesic activity and an anti-inflammatory action attributed to cyclooxygenase inhibition, and may modulate central serotonin, norepinephrine, GABA and glycine.

relative: Concurrent oral anticoagulant therapy without close INR monitoring

preg: Data are limited; use only if the potential benefit outweighs the risk. Some sources regard it as unsafe in pregnancy.
lact: Potential neonatal exposure via breast milk - use with caution during breastfeeding.
renal: Use cautiously with dose reduction in renal impairment; avoid in severe renal disease.
hepatic: Hepatically metabolized; contraindicated in severe liver disease. Transient transaminase elevations have been reported and normalize on stopping. Monitor LFTs on prolonged therapy and avoid concurrent hepatotoxins (e.g., acetaminophen). Discontinue if liver dysfunction develops.

major: Oral anticoagulants (warfarin / coumarins) - phenyramidol inhibits their metabolism, potentiating the anticoagulant effect with bleeding risk; INR rises within ~3 days and effect persists ~7 days - monitor INR and reduce anticoagulant dose as needed
Phenytoin - phenyramidol inhibits phenytoin metabolism, raising plasma levels and toxicity risk
moderate: CNS depressants and alcohol - additive sedation
Tolbutamide - inhibited metabolism, increased hypoglycemia risk
interactions.food: Take after meals to reduce gastrointestinal upset.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol - additive central nervous system depression (sedation).
interactions.diagnostics: May cause transient elevation of liver transaminases.

serious: Hepatotoxicity (transient transaminase elevation; serious liver injury reported in overdose)

monitoring: INR/prothrombin time in patients on warfarin or coumarin anticoagulants
Liver function tests, especially with prolonged use
Blood glucose if on tolbutamide; degree of sedation
counsel: May cause drowsiness or dizziness - avoid driving or operating machinery until you know how it affects you
Avoid alcohol and other sedating medicines
If you take a blood thinner (warfarin), report any unusual bruising or bleeding and keep your INR appointments
Report dark urine or yellowing of skin/eyes (possible liver effect)
pk: Analgesia within ~15 minutes; effect generally within 1 hour
Store at room temperature per manufacturer
pearls: NOT currently FDA-approved - approved in the US in 1960 (Analexin) but withdrawn; still marketed abroad (e.g., Turkey as feniramidol, brand Cabral)
Key interaction: inhibits metabolism of warfarin/coumarins (bleeding risk) and phenytoin (toxicity) - monitor INR and phenytoin levels
Acts on polysynaptic spinal reflexes without affecting neuromuscular transmission
Transient liver enzyme elevations can occur; monitor LFTs on prolonged use
missed: No specific missed-dose instruction is documented. General guidance: take the missed dose when remembered unless it is nearly time for the next dose, in which case skip it; do not double the dose.
overdose: High-dose ingestion has caused liver enzyme elevation and hepatotoxicity, and exaggerated CNS depression (sedation) would be expected. Management is supportive, with monitoring of liver function and level of consciousness; in patients on anticoagulants, monitor for bleeding.
